overview: This bill creates the Historic Greenwood District—Black Wall Street National Monument in Tulsa, Oklahoma, as part of the National Park System. Greenwood was a thriving Black business district known as Black Wall Street until the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, when a white mob destroyed much of it and killed many residents. The monument would preserve and tell the story of the district and the massacre, and it would officially come into being once the Interior Department has acquired enough land, which it may do only by donation, exchange, or purchase from willing sellers. The bill protects the rights of private property owners in and near the monument. It also sets up an 11-member unpaid advisory commission, seven of whose members must be descendants of people who lived or worked in Greenwood in 1921, to advise on the monument's development for 10 years. The Senate passed it in May 2025, and as of September 10, 2026, it had been sent to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
for: Supporters say a national monument would preserve and teach a painful but important chapter of American history that was long overlooked, and give descendants of Greenwood residents a voice in how it is told.
against: Critics say a new park unit adds to the National Park Service's costs and maintenance backlog, and some may prefer that the site be preserved and run by local or private groups.
